stem: A solution turns red litmus blue, its pH is likely to be
solution:
Red litmus is turned blue by a **base**, so the solution must be basic — and a basic solution has a **pH greater than 7**.

- (A) 1, (B) 4 and (C) 5 are all below 7, so each of these is an acidic solution and would leave red litmus red.
- **(D) 10** is above 7, so this is the only basic option.
groundedIn: §2.1.1 with Table 2.1 (red litmus turns blue in a base) and §2.3, where values less than 7 on the pH scale represent an acidic solution and values above 7 an increasingly alkaline one.

stem: A solution reacts with crushed egg-shells to give a gas that turns lime-water milky. The solution contains
solution:
Egg-shells are made of **calcium carbonate**. A gas that turns lime water milky is **carbon dioxide** — the milkiness is a white precipitate of calcium carbonate:

\(\text{Ca(OH)}_2(aq) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_3(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)

Carbon dioxide is released from a carbonate only by an **acid**:

\(\text{CaCO}_3(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + \text{CO}_2(g)\)

- **(B) HCl** is the only acid among the four options.
- (A) NaCl, (C) LiCl and (D) KCl are all neutral salts and do not react with calcium carbonate.
groundedIn: §2.1.3 and Activity 2.5, which pass the gas evolved from a carbonate through lime water and record the white precipitate; the general form is metal carbonate + acid → salt + carbon dioxide + water.

stem: 10 mL of a solution of NaOH is found to be completely neutralised by 8 mL of a given solution of HCl. If we take 20 mL of the same solution of NaOH, the amount HCl solution (the same solution as before) required to neutralise it will be
solution:
Neutralisation is a fixed-proportion reaction:

\(\text{NaOH}(aq) + \text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{NaCl}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)

Both solutions are unchanged, so the **same volume ratio holds**. Doubling the volume of base doubles the amount of acid needed:

10 mL NaOH \(\rightarrow\) 8 mL HCl

20 mL NaOH \(\rightarrow\) \(2 \times 8 = 16\) mL HCl

So **(D) 16 mL**.
groundedIn: §2.1.4 How do Acids and Bases React with each other?, which gives the neutralisation reaction between sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid and states that the effect of a base is nullified by an acid and vice versa.

stem: Which one of the following types of medicines is used for treating indigestion?
solution:
During indigestion the stomach produces **too much hydrochloric acid**, which causes pain and irritation. The remedy is a **base that neutralises the excess acid**.

- **(C) Antacid** — a mild base such as magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia) that neutralises the excess stomach acid. This is the answer.
- (A) Antibiotic kills bacteria.
- (B) Analgesic relieves pain.
- (D) Antiseptic prevents infection of a wound.
groundedIn: §2.3.1 Importance of pH in Everyday Life, under “pH in our digestive system”, which names antacids and magnesium hydroxide as the remedy for excess stomach acid.

stem: Write word equations and then balanced equations for the reaction taking place when — dilute sulphuric acid reacts with zinc granules.
solution:
**Word equation**

Zinc + Sulphuric acid \(\rightarrow\) Zinc sulphate + Hydrogen

**Balanced equation**

\(\text{Zn}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{ZnSO}_4(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\)
groundedIn: §2.1.2 How do Acids and Bases React with Metals? with Activity 2.3, which gives the general form acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas and has the reader repeat the reaction with several acids.

stem: Write word equations and then balanced equations for the reaction taking place when — dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with magnesium ribbon.
solution:
**Word equation**

Magnesium + Hydrochloric acid \(\rightarrow\) Magnesium chloride + Hydrogen

**Balanced equation**

\(\text{Mg}(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\)
groundedIn: §2.1.2 How do Acids and Bases React with Metals? with Activity 2.3, which gives the general form acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas and has the reader repeat the reaction with several acids.

stem: Write word equations and then balanced equations for the reaction taking place when — dilute sulphuric acid reacts with aluminium powder.
solution:
**Word equation**

Aluminium + Sulphuric acid \(\rightarrow\) Aluminium sulphate + Hydrogen

**Balanced equation**

\(2\text{Al}(s) + 3\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3(aq) + 3\text{H}_2(g)\)

Aluminium is trivalent, so its sulphate is \(\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3\) — which is why this equation needs coefficients where the zinc and magnesium ones did not.
groundedIn: §2.1.2 How do Acids and Bases React with Metals? with Activity 2.3, which gives the general form acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas and has the reader repeat the reaction with several acids.

stem: Write word equations and then balanced equations for the reaction taking place when — dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with iron filings.
solution:
**Word equation**

Iron + Hydrochloric acid \(\rightarrow\) Iron(II) chloride + Hydrogen

**Balanced equation**

\(\text{Fe}(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{FeCl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\)

Dilute hydrochloric acid gives iron(II) chloride, \(\text{FeCl}_2\), not \(\text{FeCl}_3\).
groundedIn: §2.1.2 How do Acids and Bases React with Metals? with Activity 2.3, which gives the general form acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas and has the reader repeat the reaction with several acids.

subtopic: Chemical Properties of Acids and Bases
stem: Compounds such as alcohols and glucose also contain hydrogen but are not categorised as acids. Describe an Activity to prove it.
solution:
The activity tests whether the compound **produces hydrogen ions in water**, which is what acidity means — not merely whether it contains hydrogen.

**Method**

- Take solutions of glucose, alcohol, hydrochloric acid and sulphuric acid.
- Fix two nails on a cork and place the cork in a 100 mL beaker.
- Connect the nails to the two terminals of a 6 volt battery through a bulb and a switch.
- Pour dilute \(\text{HCl}\) into the beaker and switch on the current. Repeat with dilute sulphuric acid, then separately with the glucose and alcohol solutions.

**Observation**

The bulb **glows** for hydrochloric acid and sulphuric acid, but **does not glow** for glucose or alcohol.

**Conclusion**

A glowing bulb means current is flowing, and the current is carried by ions. The acids therefore release \(\text{H}^+(aq)\) ions in water, while glucose and alcohol — although they contain hydrogen — do not. Since acidic character comes from \(\text{H}^+(aq)\) ions, glucose and alcohol are not acids.
groundedIn: Activity 2.8 with Fig. 2.3, which sets up exactly this conductivity test, and §2.2, which draws the conclusion that acids produce \(\text{H}^+(aq)\) in solution.

subtopic: Chemical Properties of Acids and Bases
stem: Why does distilled water not conduct electricity, whereas rain water does?
solution:
Electric current is carried through a solution by **ions**, so a liquid conducts only if it contains them.

- **Distilled water** is pure water. It contains no dissolved acids, bases or salts, so there are effectively no free ions to carry a current and it does not conduct.
- **Rain water** falls through the atmosphere and dissolves gases such as carbon dioxide and the oxides of sulphur and nitrogen. These form acids in the water, which release \(\text{H}^+(aq)\) ions. Rain water is therefore slightly acidic — acidic enough to be called acid rain when its pH drops below 5.6 — and the ions in it carry a current.
groundedIn: §2.2 (the electric current is carried through an acidic solution by ions, Activity 2.8) read with §2.3.1, which states that rain water with a pH below 5.6 is acid rain.

subtopic: Chemical Properties of Acids and Bases
stem: Why do acids not show acidic behaviour in the absence of water?
solution:
Acidic behaviour is caused by **hydrogen ions, \(\text{H}^+(aq)\)**, and an acid produces those only by **dissociating in water**:

\(\text{HCl} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2\text{O}} \text{H}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq)\)

With no water present the acid molecule does not ionise, no \(\text{H}^+\) ions are released, and so none of the acidic properties appear — dry \(\text{HCl}\) gas does not turn dry litmus red, and it does not conduct electricity.
groundedIn: Activity 2.9 and §2.2.1 What Happens to an Acid or a Base in a Water Solution?, which establish that an acid gives hydrogen ions only in aqueous solution.

stem: Five solutions A, B, C, D and E when tested with universal indicator showed pH as 4, 1, 11, 7 and 9, respectively. Which solution is neutral?
solution:
**Solution D.**

The pH of a neutral solution is exactly 7, and D is the solution with pH 7.
groundedIn: §2.3 How Strong are Acid or Base Solutions?, which sets the neutral point at pH 7, reads values below 7 as acidic and above 7 as alkaline, and states that the higher the hydronium ion concentration the lower the pH; Fig. 2.6.

stem: Five solutions A, B, C, D and E when tested with universal indicator showed pH as 4, 1, 11, 7 and 9, respectively. Which solution is strongly alkaline?
solution:
**Solution C.**

Both C (pH 11) and E (pH 9) are alkaline, since both lie above 7. C lies **further** above 7, so it is the strongly alkaline one.
groundedIn: §2.3 How Strong are Acid or Base Solutions?, which sets the neutral point at pH 7, reads values below 7 as acidic and above 7 as alkaline, and states that the higher the hydronium ion concentration the lower the pH; Fig. 2.6.

stem: Five solutions A, B, C, D and E when tested with universal indicator showed pH as 4, 1, 11, 7 and 9, respectively. Which solution is strongly acidic?
solution:
**Solution B.**

Both B (pH 1) and A (pH 4) are acidic, since both lie below 7. B lies **further** below 7, so it is the strongly acidic one.
groundedIn: §2.3 How Strong are Acid or Base Solutions?, which sets the neutral point at pH 7, reads values below 7 as acidic and above 7 as alkaline, and states that the higher the hydronium ion concentration the lower the pH; Fig. 2.6.

stem: Five solutions A, B, C, D and E when tested with universal indicator showed pH as 4, 1, 11, 7 and 9, respectively. Which solution is weakly acidic?
solution:
**Solution A.**

A has pH 4 — below 7, so acidic, but much closer to neutral than B at pH 1.
groundedIn: §2.3 How Strong are Acid or Base Solutions?, which sets the neutral point at pH 7, reads values below 7 as acidic and above 7 as alkaline, and states that the higher the hydronium ion concentration the lower the pH; Fig. 2.6.

stem: Five solutions A, B, C, D and E when tested with universal indicator showed pH as 4, 1, 11, 7 and 9, respectively. Which solution is weakly alkaline?
solution:
**Solution E.**

E has pH 9 — above 7, so alkaline, but much closer to neutral than C at pH 11.
groundedIn: §2.3 How Strong are Acid or Base Solutions?, which sets the neutral point at pH 7, reads values below 7 as acidic and above 7 as alkaline, and states that the higher the hydronium ion concentration the lower the pH; Fig. 2.6.

stem: Five solutions A, B, C, D and E when tested with universal indicator showed pH as 4, 1, 11, 7 and 9, respectively. Arrange the pH in increasing order of hydrogen-ion concentration.
solution:
The higher the hydrogen ion concentration, the **lower** the pH. So arranging in **increasing** order of hydrogen-ion concentration means arranging in **decreasing** order of pH.

Listing the pH values that way:

\(11 < 9 < 7 < 4 < 1\)

which is the order of the solutions

**C \(<\) E \(<\) D \(<\) A \(<\) B**

C, at pH 11, has the least hydrogen-ion concentration and B, at pH 1, the greatest.
groundedIn: §2.3 How Strong are Acid or Base Solutions?, which sets the neutral point at pH 7, reads values below 7 as acidic and above 7 as alkaline, and states that the higher the hydronium ion concentration the lower the pH; Fig. 2.6.

stem: Equal lengths of magnesium ribbons are taken in test tubes A and B. Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is added to test tube A, while acetic acid (CH₃COOH) is added to test tube B. Amount and concentration taken for both the acids are same. In which test tube will the fizzing occur more vigorously and why?
solution:
**The fizzing is more vigorous in test tube A**, the one holding hydrochloric acid.

The fizzing is hydrogen gas being released:

\(\text{Mg}(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\)

The rate at which it comes off depends on the **concentration of \(\text{H}^+\) ions** available, and that is where the two acids differ. At the same concentration, hydrochloric acid and acetic acid produce **different amounts of hydrogen ions**: \(\text{HCl}\) is a **strong acid** and gives many more \(\text{H}^+\) ions, while \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\) is a **weak acid** and gives far fewer.

More hydrogen ions in A means hydrogen is displaced faster there, so the fizzing is more vigorous in A than in B.
groundedIn: §2.3, which compares hydrochloric acid and acetic acid at the same concentration and states that acids giving rise to more \(\text{H}^+\) ions are strong acids and those giving fewer are weak acids; §2.1.2 for the metal-acid reaction.

stem: Fresh milk has a pH of 6. How do you think the pH will change as it turns into curd? Explain your answer.
solution:
**The pH falls below 6** — the milk becomes more acidic as it sets into curd.

When milk turns into curd, **lactic acid** is produced in it. Adding acid raises the hydrogen ion concentration, and a higher hydrogen ion concentration means a lower pH.

So the pH moves down from 6, which is why curd tastes sour.
groundedIn: Table 2.3 Some naturally occurring acids, which names lactic acid as the acid in sour milk (curd), read with §2.3: higher the hydronium ion concentration, lower is the pH value.

subtopic: Common Salt and Chemicals from It
stem: A milkman adds a very small amount of baking soda to fresh milk. Why does he shift the pH of the fresh milk from 6 to slightly alkaline?
solution:
Baking soda, sodium hydrogencarbonate, is a **mild base**. Adding a little of it neutralises some of the acid already in the milk and shifts its pH from 6 to slightly above 7.

Milk turns sour because **lactic acid** builds up in it. In a slightly alkaline milk that acid must first be used up neutralising the added base before the milk can turn acidic at all, so the souring is **delayed** and the milk keeps fresh for longer.
groundedIn: Table 2.3 (lactic acid in curd) with §2.4.3 Chemicals from Common Salt, under “Baking soda”, which describes sodium hydrogencarbonate as a mild non-corrosive basic salt used to neutralise an acid.

subtopic: Common Salt and Chemicals from It
stem: A milkman adds a very small amount of baking soda to fresh milk. Why does this milk take a long time to set as curd?
solution:
Curd sets only when the milk has become **sufficiently acidic**.

The baking soda has made the milk slightly alkaline, so the lactic acid produced as the milk sours is **spent first on neutralising that base**. Only after the base has been used up can further lactic acid start lowering the pH into the acidic range that curd needs.

That extra step is why the milk takes a long time to set as curd.
groundedIn: Table 2.3 (lactic acid in curd) with §2.4.3 Chemicals from Common Salt, under “Baking soda”, which describes sodium hydrogencarbonate as a mild non-corrosive basic salt used to neutralise an acid.

stem: Plaster of Paris should be stored in a moisture-proof container. Explain why?
solution:
Plaster of Paris is calcium sulphate hemihydrate, \(\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O}\). On mixing with water it **takes up water of crystallisation and changes back into gypsum**, setting into a hard solid mass:

\(\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O} + 1\tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

Moisture in the air is enough to start this. If Plaster of Paris is not kept in a moisture-proof container it absorbs that moisture, hardens into a useless lump of gypsum in storage, and can no longer be used for setting fractured bones or making casts.
groundedIn: §2.4.4, under “Plaster of Paris”: it is a white powder which on mixing with water changes to gypsum once again, giving a hard solid mass.

stem: What is a neutralisation reaction? Give two examples.
solution:
**A neutralisation reaction is the reaction between an acid and a base to give a salt and water.** In it the effect of the base is nullified by the acid and the effect of the acid by the base. In general:

Base + Acid \(\rightarrow\) Salt + Water

**Example 1 — sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid**

\(\text{NaOH}(aq) + \text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{NaCl}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)

**Example 2 — an antacid neutralising stomach acid**

\(\text{Mg(OH)}_2(aq) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)

Magnesium hydroxide, milk of magnesia, is the mild base used to neutralise the excess hydrochloric acid produced by the stomach during indigestion.
groundedIn: §2.1.4 How do Acids and Bases React with each other?, which names and defines the neutralisation reaction and gives the sodium hydroxide example, read with §2.3.1 “pH in our digestive system” for magnesium hydroxide as an antacid.

subtopic: Common Salt and Chemicals from It
stem: Give two important uses of washing soda and baking soda.
solution:
**Washing soda — sodium carbonate decahydrate, \(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O}\)**

- It is used in the **glass, soap and paper industries**.
- It is used for **removing the permanent hardness of water**.

**Baking soda — sodium hydrogencarbonate, \(\text{NaHCO}_3\)**

- It is used for **making baking powder**, a mixture of baking soda and a mild edible acid such as tartaric acid. On heating, the carbon dioxide it releases makes bread and cake rise and turn soft and spongy.
- It is an **ingredient in antacids**: being alkaline it neutralises excess acid in the stomach and gives relief.
groundedIn: §2.4.3 Chemicals from Common Salt — “Uses of washing soda” items (i) and (iv), and “Uses of Baking soda” items (i) and (ii).
